chapter_title: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
learning_objective: The learner will interpret a line chart of the share of the world's people who could read from 1820 to today, answering at least 2 of 3 prediction questions correctly before each answer is revealed.
specification:
Type: chart **sim-id:** world-literacy-over-time
**Library:** Chart.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** interpret
**Learning Objective:** The learner will interpret a line chart of the share of the world's people who could read from 1820 to today, answering at least 2 of 3 prediction questions correctly before each answer is revealed. **Prerequisites:** literacy, functional literacy, the 1820 and present-day literacy estimates, the UNESCO estimate of adults who cannot read (all defined in the section "Literacy" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner answers three prediction questions, each locked in before the relevant part of the chart is revealed. An answer is correct when it matches the value computed from the data under Rules. Mastery is 2 of 3 correct. Hovering over data points after the reveal is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Most people have been able to read since the invention of printing. (2) Mass literacy is centuries old in most of the world. (3) Illiteracy is now so rare it no longer matters. **Instructional Rationale:** A prediction before the reveal exposes the learner's mental timeline of literacy, and seeing the gap between prediction and data is what makes the steep 20th-century rise memorable. Three questions cover the starting level, the timing of the change, and the size of what remains. **Content:** A single line: share of the world population that is literate (percent), for every year the source provides from 1820 to the latest year. The share that is not literate is shown as the area above the line. Two labeled event markers: 1821, Sequoyah completes the Cherokee syllabary; 1928, Turkey adopts the Latin-based alphabet (Day 5). Prediction questions, in this order: | # | Question | Choices | How the correct answer is found | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | In 1820, what share of the world's people could read? | Under 25%; 25–50%; 50–75%; Over 75% | The 1820 value in the data | | 2 | In which period did more than half the world first become literate? | 1820–1869; 1870–1919; 1920–1969; 1970–2020 | The period containing the first data year whose value is >= 50% | | 3 | Today about 750 million adults cannot read. Roughly what share of the world's adults is that? | About 5%; About 10–15%; About 30%; About 50% | 750 million divided by 6.1 billion adults (aged 15 and over) is about 12%, so "About 10–15%" | **Provenance:** Literacy shares from Our World in Data, "Literate and illiterate world population" (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/literate-and-illiterate-world-population); download its CSV and copy the World series into the sim folder, keeping the source and download date with the data. The 750 million figure is UNESCO's estimate of adults lacking basic literacy (chapter section "Literacy," "roughly three-quarters of a billion"). The 6.1 billion adults aged 15 and over is an approximate figure derived from the UN World Population Prospects 2024; the sim labels it "approximate." Event dates come from the chapter sections "Writing Systems" (Cherokee, about 1821) and "The Alphabet" (1928). **Rules:** Question 1 uses the 1820 value; if the source has no 1820 value, use its earliest year and name that year in the question. Question 2 uses the first data year whose literate share is >= 50%; a year that falls exactly on a period boundary belongs to the period it begins. Question 3's answer is fixed as "About 10–15%" from the arithmetic shown. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees an empty chart frame from 1820 to today and question 1. They choose an answer; the 1820 point appears and is marked correct or not. 2. For question 2, the learner chooses a period; the full line draws, and the year it crosses 50% is marked. 3. For question 3, the learner chooses a share; the remaining gap above the latest point is labeled with the UNESCO estimate. 4. After all three, the learner can hover over any point to see its year and value, and over the two event markers. 5. The learner should notice how flat the line is for the 19th century and how steep it becomes in the 20th. **Feedback:** Three questions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Right." plus a one-sentence explanation using the data value. Incorrect: "Not quite: ." plus the same explanation, which names the misconception: (1) printing made books cheaper, but most people still had no school; (2) mass literacy is mostly a 20th-century achievement; (3) the share is small but the number is about three-quarters of a billion people, nearly two-thirds of them women. A score "Predictions correct: n of 3" is shown. **Starting State:** Empty axes (years 1820 to today, 0–100%), the two event markers, and question 1 with the prompt "Before we look: how many people could read two hundred years ago?" **Chapter Anchors:** Fewer than one person in eight could read around 1820; close to nine in ten adults today. UNESCO: roughly three-quarters of a billion adults cannot read, nearly two-thirds of them women. 1928 Turkish alphabet reform. If the downloaded 1820 value is not between 10% and 13%, flag the difference to the author.
